At the myocardial level, ionizing radiation promotes endothelial dysfunction, microvascular rarefaction, chronic inflammation, and progressive interstitial fibrosis, ultimately impairing RV contractile mechanics. Simultaneously, radiation-induced lung injury contributes to pulmonary vascular remodeling, increased pulmonary vascular resistance, and RV-pulmonary artery uncoupling, further accelerating RV dysfunction. Contemporary multimodality imaging has substantially improved detection of these alterations in their subclinical phase. Advanced echocardiographic techniques, particularly RV free-wall longitudinal strain, enable early identification of mechanical abnormalities before conventional indices become abnormal. Cardiac magnetic resonance provides a highly reproducible assessment of RV volumes and function and offers unique capabilities for myocardial deformation analysis, tissue characterization, and quantification of diffuse fibrosis through extracellular volume mapping. Cardiac computed tomography has emerged as a critical tool for cardiac substructure dosimetry, facilitating personalized RT planning and RV sparing strategies. In parallel, radiomics and artificial intelligence approaches are opening new opportunities for individualized risk prediction and long-term surveillance. This narrative review summarizes the current understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying radiation-induced RV injury, critically examines the role of multimodality imaging in its detection and monitoring, and proposes an integrated clinical framework to improve early diagnosis, risk stratification, and prevention of RV dysfunction in patients exposed to thoracic RT.

title: HIGH-DOSE TARGETED RADIATION FOLLOWED BY CHEMOIMMUNOTHERAPY FOR ADVANCED BILE-DUCT CANCER IN HOUSTON'S SAFETY-NET POPULATION
summary:
The purpose of this study is to learn whether a treatment sequence of high-dose radiation followed by chemotherapy and immunotherapy can be delivered safely and on schedule to patients with bile duct cancer (cholangiocarcinoma) inside the liver that cannot be removed with surgery.

Participants first receive targeted, high-dose radiation therapy to the liver tumor over 15 treatments (about 3 weeks), with capecitabine, an oral chemotherapy pill taken on radiation days to make the radiation more effective. After a 4 to 6 week recovery and restaging period, participants receive the standard combination of durvalumab (an immunotherapy), gemcitabine, and cisplatin for up to 8 cycles, followed by durvalumab alone as maintenance. All treatments are FDA-approved and used as standard care; the study evaluates the order in which they are given.

The main question is whether at least 9 of 12 participants can complete radiation and start chemoimmunotherapy within 8 weeks. The study also tracks side effects, tumor control, survival, quality of life, and barriers to care. It is enrolling at Harris Health System and Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center in Houston, Texas.

title: Generalized Myasthenia Gravis Identified During Evaluation for Streptococcal Pharyngitis: A Case Report.
authors: Memari K, Yanover B, Rodriguez SA et al.
abstract: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction characterized by fluctuating skeletal muscle weakness that worsens with exertion and improves with rest. Ocular manifestations, including ptosis and diplopia, are common early features, but generalized disease may also involve bulbar, limb, axial, or respiratory muscles. Because symptoms may be intermittent or occur alongside common acute illnesses, first-contact clinicians must avoid prematurely attributing fatigue or malaise to a concurrent infection when focal fatigable weakness is present. We present a case of a 50-year-old woman with hypertension, obesity, postmenopausal bleeding, and 12 lb of unintentional weight loss over three months who presented to an outpatient clinic with upper respiratory symptoms and generalized fatigue. Rapid antigen testing was positive for group A Streptococcus, and antibiotic therapy with amoxicillin was initiated. During the same evaluation, she reported several weeks of progressive right eyelid drooping, intermittent diplopia, worsening fatigue later in the day, evening gait difficulty, and slurred speech that became more noticeable during prolonged conversations. Examination demonstrated right-sided ptosis, preserved pupillary responses, and ocular misalignment worsened by sustained upward gaze. The ice-pack test improved right margin reflex distance 1 from 1 mm to 4 mm after two minutes of cooling. Given the combination of ocular, bulbar, and limb fatigability, the presentation was classified as generalized myasthenia gravis, Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America class IIb. Acetylcholine receptor binding antibody was elevated at 8.6 nmol/L, repetitive nerve stimulation demonstrated a 17% decrement in compound muscle action potential amplitude with 3-Hz stimulation of the right facial nerve recording from the nasalis, and chest computed tomography showed no thymoma. Pyridostigmine was initiated at 30 mg orally three times daily and later increased to 60 mg three times daily as tolerated, with improvement in ptosis and dysarthria at two-week follow-up. This case highlights the importance of recognizing generalized myasthenia gravis when fatigable ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, and end-of-day weakness coexist with a common acute infection. Streptococcal pharyngitis explained the patient's upper respiratory symptoms but did not explain the pattern of fluctuating ocular and bulbar weakness. Bedside fatigability testing, careful differential diagnosis, medication review, and urgent neurology referral are essential because infection can precipitate clinical worsening and myasthenic crisis.

title: In vivo screening identifies SLC38A3 as a metabolic booster for CAR T cell therapy
summary: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are highly effective against certain blood cancers, but struggle in the hostile tumor microenvironment (TME) of solid tumors. We developed the CARGO method for in vivo gain-of-function screening in CAR T cells and used it to equip CAR T cells with enhanced access to nutrients inside the TME, by overexpressing 452 solute carrier (SLC) transmembrane transporters. We identified SLC38A3, a sodium-coupled amino acid transporter not endogenously expressed in T cells, as an effective booster of CAR T cell performance in xenograft models of hepatocellular carcinoma (Huh7, HepG2) and ovarian adenocarcinoma (SKOV3). Ectopic expression of SLC38A3 in CAR T cells enhanced their glutamine uptake, improved metabolic fitness, and promoted a stem-like memory phenotype, which resulted in superior antitumor efficacy and durable protection upon tumor rechallenge in glutamine-restricted solid tumors. In summary, our study shows that equipping CAR T cells with non-native nutrient transporters can confer enhanced metabolic resilience, and it establishes the feasibility and utility of in vivo open reading frame (ORF) screens in CAR T cells to tackle the hostile TME of solid tumors.

title: CD33-CAR iNKT cells overcome acute myeloid leukemia heterogeneity by activating CD8+ T cells and enhancing tumor immunogenicity
summary: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) exhibits extensive inter- and intra-patient antigenic heterogeneity, representing a major obstacle for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based therapies. Cellular platforms that combine potent direct cytotoxicity with the ability to engage endogenous immune responses may help overcome this limitation. Invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells are particularly attractive for allogeneic immunotherapy because of their lack of alloreactivity and their capacity to promote cross-priming of conventional T cells. To exploit these properties in AML, we generated CD33-directed CAR iNKT cells and demonstrated direct antitumor activity against CD33-expressing AML cells both in vitro and in vivo. Using an in vitro mixed-tumor model composed of parental CD33-expressing and CD33-knockout MOLM-14 cells we show that CD33-CAR iNKT cells efficiently eliminated CD33-positive leukemia cells but did not directly control the growth of CD33-knockout cells. However, the addition of conventional T cells, particularly CD8 T cells, together with CD33-CAR iNKT cells resulted in robust T-cell activation and subsequent control of CD33-knockout MOLM-14 cells. Importantly, CD33-CAR iNKT cells induced marked phenotypic changes in antigen-negative leukemia cells, including upregulation of HLA class I and class II molecules, suggesting increased immunogenicity. Finally, we recapitulated both the antitumor and immunomodulatory effects of CD33-CAR iNKT cells in primary bone marrow samples from patients with newly diagnosed AML. Collectively, these findings show that CD33-CAR iNKT cells can promote CD8 T-cell immunity against AML and support a therapeutic strategy capable of extending antitumor activity beyond the targeted antigen, thereby helping to overcome antigenic heterogeneity.
